summary: The transcript presents a unified framework in which specifications serve as a universal language of intent across disciplines. Programmers use code specifications to align silicon hardware behavior, product managers use product specifications to align team efforts, and lawmakers use legal specifications to align human behavior. Sean Grove argues that when anyone writes a prompt for an AI model, they are creating a protospecification—a preliminary specification that aligns an AI model toward a common set of intentions and values. This reframing positions prompt authors as spec authors, regardless of whether they consciously recognize that role. The practical benefits emphasized are that specs enable faster and safer shipping of work and that they democratize contribution, since everyone can participate. A striking claim is that whoever writes the spec becomes the programmer, erasing traditional boundaries between roles such as PM, lawmaker, engineer, or marketer. The central thesis is that specification authorship is the universal act underlying all alignment work, from silicon to humans to AI models, and that recognizing this shared activity creates a common language across seemingly disparate fields. This perspective elevates prompting from a narrow technical activity to a broader act of intent expression, positioning all spec authors as programmers in a universal sense.
